cards.front: Why is biotransformation needed for drug elimination?
cards.back: Most drugs are lipid soluble and would be reabsorbed in renal tubules and persist for a long time. Metabolism converts them into polar, ionised products that kidney and bile can clear.

cards.front: Where does drug metabolism mainly occur, and which other organs contribute?
cards.back: Liver is the main site. Kidney, intestinal wall, lungs and plasma also metabolise drugs.

cards.front: Compare phase I and phase II drug metabolism.
cards.back: Phase I (functionalisation: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) adds or exposes a polar group; the product may be active or inactive. Phase II (conjugation) attaches an endogenous polar molecule, usually giving an inactive, excretable product. Morphine-6-glucuronide is a notable active conjugate.

cards.front: Which CYP450 isoform metabolises the largest share of drugs, and name two inhibitors of it.
cards.back: CYP3A4/5, which handles roughly half of all drugs. Inhibitors include erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice.

cards.front: Which CYP isoform forms the toxic metabolite of paracetamol, and what induces it?
cards.back: CYP2E1 converts paracetamol to the reactive metabolite NAPQI. Chronic alcohol use and isoniazid induce CYP2E1. Glutathione conjugation normally detoxifies NAPQI; depletion leads to hepatotoxicity.

cards.front: What is the most important conjugation pathway in drug metabolism?
cards.back: Glucuronidation by UDP-glucuronosyl transferases (UGTs), acting on -OH and -COOH groups. Glucuronides excreted in bile can be cleaved by gut bacteria and reabsorbed, causing enterohepatic cycling.

cards.front: Describe the time course of microsomal enzyme induction.
cards.back: Metabolic rate rises about 2 to 4 fold as enzyme synthesis increases. The peak develops over about 4 to 14 days while the inducer is given, and activity returns to baseline over roughly 1 to 3 weeks after withdrawal.

cards.front: Define first-pass metabolism and give the formula for oral bioavailability.
cards.back: First-pass (presystemic) metabolism is metabolism of an orally given drug in the gut wall (CYP3A4 is expressed in intestine) and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation. Oral F = fraction absorbed x (1 - hepatic extraction ratio). Sublingual, transdermal and parenteral routes avoid it; rectal avoids it only partly.

cards.front: How does urine pH affect renal excretion of weak acids and weak bases?
cards.back: Only un-ionised drug is reabsorbed from the tubule. Weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine and weak bases in acidic urine. Urine is alkalinised in barbiturate and salicylate poisoning. Acidifying urine could speed excretion of bases (morphine, amphetamine) but is not practised, because acidosis can cause rhabdomyolysis and cardiotoxicity.

cards.front: Define clearance and give its formula.
cards.back: Clearance is the theoretical volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time. CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration.

cards.front: Give the formula for elimination half-life and state how many half-lives are needed for near-complete elimination.
cards.back: t1/2 = 0.693 x V / CL. It is a derived value and is constant only for first-order elimination. About 4 to 5 half-lives are needed for nearly complete elimination (about 94 percent after four).

cards.front: Write the formula for a loading dose and say what it depends on.
cards.back: Loading dose = target plasma concentration x V / F. It depends on volume of distribution and bioavailability, not on clearance or half-life.

cards.front: Short note: Microsomal enzyme induction

points: Drugs, chemicals and some dietary agents increase synthesis of microsomal enzymes, mainly CYP450 and UGT
Metabolic rate rises about 2 to 4 fold
Peak develops over about 4 to 14 days
Reverses over about 1 to 3 weeks after withdrawal
Phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine (CYP3A)
Rifampin (broad induction)
Chronic alcohol and isoniazid (CYP2E1)
Cigarette smoke and charbroiled meat (CYP1A)
Oral contraceptive failure with rifampin
Loss of nevirapine effect with rifampin; autoinduction by carbamazepine
Increased paracetamol hepatotoxicity
Precipitation of acute intermittent porphyria
Phenobarbitone for congenital non-haemolytic jaundice
Phenytoin in some cases of Cushing syndrome

cards.front: Short note: First-pass (presystemic) metabolism

points: Metabolism of an orally given drug in gut wall and liver before it enters systemic circulation
Hepatic extraction ratio; for high-extraction drugs, hepatic blood flow
Gut-wall CYP3A4 and liver enzyme activity
Genetic variation, enzyme induction or inhibition
High first-pass: propranolol, verapamil, morphine, pethidine, lidocaine, glyceryl trinitrate
Low first-pass: phenobarbitone, tolbutamide, theophylline, diazepam, isosorbide mononitrate
Oral dose much higher than sublingual or parenteral dose
Marked individual variation in oral bioavailability
Bioavailability rises in severe liver disease or with enzyme inhibitors
Sublingual, transdermal or parenteral routes bypass it
F = fraction absorbed x (1 - hepatic extraction ratio)

cards.front: Short note: CYP450 inhibition and drug interactions

points: Azole antifungals and macrolides bind the haem iron of CYP450
Competitive inhibition when two drugs use the same isoenzyme or cofactor
Acts quickly, unlike induction
CYP3A4: erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, verapamil, ritonavir, fluoxetine, grapefruit juice
CYP2D6: quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine
CYP2C9: fluvoxamine, fluconazole, gemfibrozil, trimethoprim; CYP2C19: omeprazole, fluconazole
CYP1A2: fluvoxamine, fluoxetine; CYP2E1: disulfiram, fomepizole
Higher plasma level of the object drug
Higher oral bioavailability of high first-pass drugs
Longer half-life when clearance falls
Toxicity with narrow-margin drugs such as warfarin and phenytoin
Quinidine is a CYP3A4 substrate but inhibits CYP2D6
Low-dose ritonavir boosts other HIV protease inhibitors through CYP3A4 inhibition
Erythromycin or ketoconazole with terfenadine, astemizole or cisapride caused dangerous arrhythmias

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

points: Narrow-margin drugs: digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides, anticonvulsants, theophylline
Large individual variation: antidepressants, lithium
Toxic drugs in renal failure
Suspected poisoning
Unexplained treatment failure or adherence check
Long-acting drugs: trough steady-state level, just before the next dose
Short-acting drugs: post-absorptive peak, about 1 to 2 h after oral or IM dose
Poisoning: early sample, then repeated to track clearance
Drugs with easily measured effect: antihypertensives, oral anticoagulants, diuretics
Prodrugs such as levodopa
Hit-and-run drugs: reserpine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole
Irreversible drugs such as organophosphates
Revised dose rate = previous dose rate x target Css / measured Css

cards.front: Short note: Prolongation of drug action

points: Less frequent dosing and better adherence
Smoother plasma levels with fewer peak-related side effects
Round-the-clock control (e.g. overnight)
Slow absorption: sustained or controlled-release oral forms, depot i.m. or s.c. injections, implants, transdermal patches
Highly protein-bound congeners released slowly (e.g. sulfadoxine)
Slower metabolism: chemical change (ethinyl estradiol vs estradiol) or enzyme inhibition (allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine; ritonavir boosting)
Reduced tubular secretion: probenecid with penicillin
Controlled-release forms suit drugs with half-life under 4 h
Not needed for drugs with half-life over 12 h (doxycycline, amlodipine) or for brief-effect drugs (hypnotics)

cards.front: Essay: Zero-order (saturable) versus first-order elimination

points: Elimination = metabolism + excretion
Clearance: volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time
Constant fraction eliminated per unit time; rate proportional to concentration
Clearance and half-life constant; plasma level falls exponentially
Applies to most drugs in the therapeutic range; dose rate and steady-state level linearly related
Constant amount eliminated per unit time once enzymes are saturated (ethyl alcohol)
Rate = Vmax x C / (Km + C)
Clearance falls and half-life lengthens as dose rises
Phenytoin, tolbutamide, theophylline and warfarin shift from first to zero order at higher doses
Plasma concentration rises disproportionately with dose (nonlinear elimination)
Small dose increments can cause toxicity; increase in small steps
Monitor plasma levels (TDM)
Know whether a drug's elimination is saturable before adjusting its dose

cards.front: Essay: Renal excretion of drugs

points: Kidney excretes water-soluble drugs and metabolites
Net excretion = (filtration + secretion) - reabsorption
All non-protein-bound drug is filtered
Depends on plasma protein binding and renal blood flow
GFR is about 120 mL/min and falls after age 50
Passive diffusion of lipid-soluble, un-ionised drug
Ionised drugs stay in the lumen, so urine pH matters
Used for ion trapping in poisoning
Active, through OAT (acids such as penicillin, probenecid, methotrexate) and OCT (bases such as procainamide, cimetidine)
Efflux pumps P-gp and MRP2 on the luminal membrane
Clearance above GFR indicates secretion
Drugs compete for the same carrier (probenecid and penicillin)
Neonates: immature tubular transport, so penicillins and cephalosporins last longer
Elderly and renal failure: lower clearance, so doses need adjustment
Creatinine clearance guides dosing in renal disease
Competition for secretion explains many drug interactions

cards.front: Essay: Factors affecting drug metabolism

points: Biotransformation by microsomal (CYP450, UGT) and nonmicrosomal enzymes
Amount and activity of enzymes vary widely between people
CYP2D6 poor and extensive metabolisers; ultrarapid genotype
N-acetyl transferase slow and fast acetylators
Up to about 6-fold variation in metabolic rate among healthy adults
Newborns, especially premature, have low enzyme activity; phase I matures within months
Conjugation takes 3 months or more to reach adult levels
Hepatic function and clearance decline in the elderly
Inhibition: azoles, macrolides, cimetidine, isoniazid
Induction: phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin
Liver disease reduces metabolism and raises oral bioavailability
Smoking, charcoal-grilled food and chronic alcohol alter CYP1A and CYP2E1
Diet can change enzyme levels
Marked interspecies differences in CYP and UGT activity, for example in cats and dogs

cards.front: Phase I and phase II biotransformation reactions
cards.text: Phase I reactions include {{oxidation}}, {{reduction}} and {{hydrolysis}}; phase II (synthetic) reactions include {{glucuronidation}}, {{acetylation}}, {{methylation}} and {{sulfation}}.

cards.front: CYP450 inducers by isoform
cards.text: Phenobarbitone, phenytoin and carbamazepine induce {{CYP3A}}; rifampin induces {{CYP3A}} and {{CYP2C}}; chronic alcohol and {{isoniazid}} induce {{CYP2E1}}; cigarette smoke induces {{CYP1A}}.

cards.front: Routes of drug excretion
cards.text: Major routes are {{urine}} (kidney), {{bile into faeces}}, {{exhaled air}} for gases and volatile agents, {{saliva and sweat}} (minor), and {{breast milk}}.

cards.front: Renal tubular transport systems
cards.text: The proximal tubule secretes organic {{acids}} through the OAT system and organic {{bases}} through the OCT system; efflux pumps {{P-gp}} and {{MRP2}} sit on the luminal membrane.

cards.front: Acetylation polymorphism
cards.text: N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) polymorphism gives {{slow}} and {{fast}} acetylator phenotypes. Acetylated drugs include {{isoniazid}}, {{hydralazine}}, procainamide, dapsone and sulfonamides; isoniazid neuropathy and hydralazine or procainamide {{lupus}} occur mainly in slow acetylators.

cards.front: Short note: Prodrugs

points: Inactive compound converted in the body to one or more active metabolites
Greater stability or better bioavailability
Better pharmacokinetic properties, fewer side effects
Selective activation at the site of action (e.g. levodopa crosses the BBB, then forms dopamine in brain)
Levodopa, enalapril, alpha-methyldopa, dipivefrine
Proguanil, prednisone, clopidogrel, bacampicillin, sulfasalazine
Cyclophosphamide, fluorouracil, mercaptopurine, acyclovir
Activation depends on metabolising enzymes, e.g. clopidogrel is a CYP2C19 substrate; codeine needs CYP2D6 to form morphine

cards.front: Maintenance dose and steady state: what is the formula, and how long does steady state take?
cards.back: Maintenance dose rate = target Css x CL / F; it depends on clearance (or half-life). With repeated dosing at a fixed rate, drug accumulates until intake equals elimination (plateau principle); steady state is reached in about 4 to 5 half-lives. A loading dose is used when waiting this long is unacceptable (digoxin, chloroquine, amiodarone).

cards.front: Microsomal vs non-microsomal drug-metabolising enzymes: how do they differ?
cards.back: Microsomal enzymes sit on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mainly of liver (also kidney, gut mucosa, lungs): CYP450 monooxygenases, UGTs, epoxide hydrolases. They carry out most oxidations, reductions, hydrolyses and glucuronidation, and are inducible. Non-microsomal enzymes lie in cytoplasm, mitochondria and plasma (esterases, amidases, some flavoprotein oxidases, most conjugases); they carry out all conjugations except glucuronidation, are not inducible, but many show genetic polymorphism (acetyltransferase, pseudocholinesterase). Hofmann elimination (atracurium) is spontaneous, non-enzymatic breakdown in body fluids.

cards.front: Short note: Zero-order kinetics of elimination

points: Elimination rate is constant whatever the plasma concentration
A constant amount is eliminated per unit time
Clearance falls as concentration rises
Ethyl alcohol (example in KDT8)
Some drugs move from first-order to zero-order at high doses, so plasma concentration rises disproportionately with dose

cards.front: Short note: Clearance of drugs

points: Theoretical volume of plasma from which the drug is completely removed in unit time (analogous to creatinine clearance)
CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacometrics in individual dosing

points: Dosing tools use pharmacokinetic models built from representative patient populations
Such tools predict an individual's dose from that patient's measured response
Compare predicted pharmacokinetic parameters with the measured concentration
Example: expected clearance 5.5 L/h; a higher measured level gives a revised clearance of 3.5 L/h, so the daily dose is halved
The implicit method is misleading before steady state
At least a week of regular dosing (four half-lives) must pass first
